headline: Bunker Blitz at the Rips: An 18-Pound Blue Wins the Tournament, Albies Show East of the Lighthouse
subhead: The bait is stacked from North Bar to Shagwong and the bass are shadowing it hard — this is the two-week window the whole season builds toward.
body_markdown:
There's a particular week every September when Montauk stops being a place you fish and becomes the place everyone in the Northeast is thinking about, and this is that week. The bunker never left the rips this summer, but now they're getting pushed — mullet and peanut schools evacuating Fort Pond Bay and the back harbors, bass and blues stacking underneath, and the whole system tightening up the way it does right before the real fall run gets its legs. We said last week this was shaping up to be the best two-week stretch of the year building at the Point, and with water running 69 degrees off the Lighthouse and a new moon tide still pushing extra water through the rips, that call is looking better every day.

The headline number this week is a bluefish — 18.49 pounds, taken off a thick bunker school working the rip current, good enough to win a tournament and good enough to tell you something real about the size class moving through right now. That's not a random cocktail blue. That's a mature fish that's been offshore all summer and just found the buffet line at the Point. The bunker schools have been holding tight to the boulder field on the building tide, and where you find bait balled up that dense, in water that clean, you find blues willing to hit anything that looks wounded — bunker spoons, 2-ounce Kastmasters, or a chunk bounced right through the school on a fish-finder rig with 40-pound leader, because these blues will bite through anything lighter.

Striped bass are the story underneath the story. They're shadowing the same bait, but they're doing it the way big fish do in September — tight to structure, patient, letting the blues and the current do the work of disorganizing the bunker before they commit. The boulder field off the Point on the incoming has been holding fish, mostly slot-class stripers in the 28 to 34-inch range with a few better ones mixed in, taken on bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range worked slow along the bottom, white or bone color, cast across the current and swum back with the sweep rather than against it. North Bar has been better on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide — that's when the rip really loads up and the bass tuck in behind the third boulder line waiting for bait to get swept over. Shagwong Reef is fishing similarly, though it wants a little more tide movement to really turn on; the dead slack there has been quiet.

And now the albies. False albacore started showing east of the Point earlier this week, which is exactly the development we flagged as coming — the same warm-water edge that's been feeding Rhode Island's albie run has pushed close enough now that Montauk boats working outside Turtle Cove and along the rip lines east of the Lighthouse are getting into them, mostly in short, violent windows when the fish push bait to the surface. It's not a sustained blitz yet — more a scattered pattern of pop-up feeds that come and go over ten or fifteen minutes — but the fact that they're here at all this early in September, with squid concentrations building up around Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound and starting to drift this way, tells you the bait highway into Montauk is fully open. Epoxy jigs and small Deadly Dicks in the half-ounce range have been the better producers when you can get in front of a feed; the trick is running light drag and covering water until you spot the nervous water or diving terns, because albies don't wait around for a slow approach.

Fluke fishing has held up better than you'd expect for mid-September, with drifts off the south side in 30 to 50 feet still turning up keepers on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the sandy stretches between structure. That bite won't last much longer — the exodus toward deeper water typically kicks in hard once the water starts a real cooldown, and we're not there yet, but the calendar says it's close.

The next 48 to 72 hours look like more of the same, maybe better. Tidal range is still building toward the new moon, which means more water moving harder through the rips, which means bait gets pushed harder and the bass commit more aggressively — that's the mechanism behind every good September at Montauk, and there's no reason to think it breaks this week. If the squid keep drifting down from the Rhode Island grounds the way the pattern suggests, that's the ingredient that turns a good bluefish week into a genuine blitz week, with bass mixing in heavier at first light and last light. If you've only got one day, fish the building tide at North Bar in the two hours before and after the top, work the boulder field methodically with bucktails rather than blind-casting the open rip, and keep a popper rigged for any surface activity that shows — because right now, at the Point, in mid-September, that surface activity can show up fast and it can be worth everything.
